A. Example and B. Sample
1 Introduction
Many people now read reports, papers and news artic-
les on a phone. A phone screen shows only a few lines of
a page that was designed for paper, so readers zoom, scr-
oll sideways and often lose their place. This study asks
whether showing a document one short phrase at a time
helps readers keep their place without changing what
they understand.
Earlier work suggests that eye movements take only a
small part of reading time, and that understanding the
language is the main limit on speed. We therefore do not
claim that phrase display makes reading faster in general.
Instead, we look at how often readers stop, go back or
give up when the layout of the original page gets in the
way.
2 Method
Twenty-four volunteers read three short reports each.
Every report was shown in two ways: as the original
two-column page, and as a sequence of short phrases in
the centre of the screen. The order of the reports and the
order of the two displays were balanced across readers.
After each report, readers answered five questions about
published elsewhere.
The documents used in this study were written for the study and are not
its content and rated how easy it was to follow.
The
phrase

running

page
numbers and footnotes, joined words that had been split
across lines, and read the left column before the right
column. Readers could pause at any time, step back one
phrase, or open the original page to look at a figure.
3 Results
Readers answered about the same number of questi-
ons correctly with both displays. They stopped less often
with the phrase display, and most said it was easier to
keep their place. Several readers preferred the original
page for sections with tables or equations, which sugge-
sts that a reader should make it easy to switch between
the two views.
These results come from a small group and from short
texts written for the study, so they should be treated as a
starting point. Larger studies with real papers and longer
reading sessions are needed before drawing firm conclus-

A. Example and B. Sample
1 Introduction

A phone screen shows only a few lines of a page that was designed for paper, so readers zoom, scroll sideways and often lose their place.
